name: The Irish Potato Famine
intro: In 1845, a plant disease called blight began destroying Ireland's potato crops. Potatoes were the main food for poor families, so millions of people went hungry and about 1 million died. About 2 million people left Ireland, and most of them sailed to the United States.

keyFacts.label: How many
keyFacts.value: About 2 million people left Ireland between 1845 and 1855

keyFacts.label: Where they went
keyFacts.value: Mostly the United States; also Canada, Great Britain, and Australia

timeline.text: Potato blight reaches Ireland, and potatoes begin to rot after the harvest.
Blight destroys most of Ireland's potato crop.
"Black '47" is the worst year. The Choctaw Nation sends $170 to help Irish families.
Ireland's census counts more than 1.5 million fewer people than in 1841.
Potato crops finally recover, and the famine is considered over.
John F. Kennedy, great-grandson of a famine immigrant, is elected U.S. president.

sections.title: What happened?
paragraphs: In the 1840s, most poor families in Ireland depended on potatoes for food. More than half of the people relied on potatoes as their main food. Many families ate almost nothing else. Farmers grew mostly one kind of potato, called the Irish Lumper.
In 1845, a plant disease called blight reached Ireland. It made potatoes rot after the harvest. In 1846, the blight destroyed almost the whole potato crop. It kept coming back until about 1852.

More than three million people depended completely on potatoes, so huge numbers of families went hungry. About 1 million people died from hunger and sickness. The year 1847 was so bad that people called it "Black '47." In Irish, the famine is called An Gorta Mór, which means "the Great Hunger."

sections.title: Why did people move?
paragraphs: Most Irish farmers were tenants who rented their land from rich landowners. Without potatoes, they had no food and very little money. Some landlords evicted families from their homes. Some even paid for ship tickets to send poor tenants away.

Ireland was ruled by Great Britain at the time. The British government bought corn from America to help, but it was not nearly enough. Meanwhile, food such as butter and livestock was still shipped out of Ireland. Many Irish people were angry that food left the country while people starved.

Families left to escape hunger and sickness and to find work. Between 1845 and 1855, more than 2 million people left Ireland. It was one of the largest movements of people from a single island in history.

sections.title: Where did they go, and how?
paragraphs: Most emigrants sailed across the Atlantic Ocean to the United States. Others went to Canada, Great Britain, or Australia. So many went to Liverpool, England, that it was called "Ireland's second capital." Many people who landed in Canada later traveled south into the United States.

The ocean trip took about 40 days. Many ships were old cargo ships that were crowded and dirty. Passengers had little food or clean water, and sickness spread quickly. Because so many passengers became sick and died, people called these ships "coffin ships."

Most Irish immigrants settled in Boston, New York, and other cities on the East Coast. Many were too poor to travel any farther than the docks. They lived in crowded buildings near the ports, often in basements and attics. Families formed close Catholic communities to help each other.

sections.title: How did it change lives?
paragraphs: Life in America was hard at first. Irish men took dangerous, low-paying jobs, like digging canals and laying railroad track. Women often worked as servants or in textile mills. Some job ads even said, "No Irish need apply."

Some Americans treated Irish immigrants unfairly because they were poor and Catholic. A political group called the Know-Nothings tried to keep immigrants out of power. Over time, though, Irish Americans became leaders in their cities. In 1960, John F. Kennedy, the great-grandson of a famine immigrant, was elected president.

The famine changed Ireland forever. Its population fell from about 8.2 million in 1841 to about 6.6 million in 1851. Today, about 32 million Americans have mostly Irish roots. Memorials in Ireland, New York City, Boston, and other places help people remember the Great Hunger.

vocab.meaning: A time when there is not enough food for many people, so they go hungry.
A plant disease that makes crops rot and die.
A person who pays rent to live on or farm someone else's land.
To force people to leave the home or land they rent.
To leave your home country to live in another country.
A person who moves to a new country to live there.
Treating people unfairly because of who they are, such as their religion or where they come from.

photos.caption: The Jeanie Johnston is a copy of a real ship that carried Irish families to North America during the famine.
